column4: A person carrying something heavy runs a quiet calculation before every conversation: how much room the other one has left this week, and whether this is worth spending it on. The answer comes back no almost every time. The thing gets carried alone, and the not-asking turns into a second weight on top of the first.
column7: My friends have their own problems. Why would I put mine on top of that?

column3: The subject nobody at home wants
column4: One subject lights a person up, and one household has heard enough of it. The subject does not go anywhere when it stops being spoken about. It goes underground and comes back out as irritation over the dishwasher.
column7: My husband finds it boring and there's nobody else. So where does it go?

column4: A story that hasn't resolved gets told again. By the fourth telling the listener has started managing their face, and the teller has started noticing them managing it. The story stops being told after that, which is a different thing from the story being finished.
column7: My friends have heard this four times already. I can't do it again.

column3: An hour that belongs to you
column4: Asked to talk about themselves, people ration. Ten minutes in they check the other face, apologise for going on, and hand the conversation back. The apology arrives long before anybody was actually bored.
column7: Is it even okay to talk about myself for a whole hour?

column4: In most circles one person has become the one you call. They're good at it, so they get more of it. Their own week goes unreported for years, and nobody notices the silence, because a good listener never leaves a gap where a gap would show.
column7: I'm always the one who listens. Who listens to me?

column4: Certain thoughts get thought for years without ever being made into a sentence. Sentences make things real and locatable, which is exactly why the thought is kept as a feeling instead. Typing it turns out easier than speaking it, and the first sentence is usually shorter than anyone expects.
column7: I can't say this out loud. Not even to myself.

column4: At forty-five a person can be carrying a question that sounds like it belongs to somebody of twenty, and the gap between the two becomes its own reason to ask nobody. The question doesn't get easier with the years. It gets more embarrassing, so it gets asked later, or never.
column7: I'm too old to still be asking something like this.

column3: Please don't feel sorry for me
column4: Sympathy arrives fast and lands wrong. Told about a hard week, most listeners reach for comfort, and comfort closes the conversation by treating it as something already finished. What was wanted was one more question.
column7: I want to complain without anyone pitying me.

column4: Advice is the cheapest thing to hand over and the easiest thing to hand over instead of listening. Somebody who has been carrying a problem for months has already heard the obvious answer from four directions. A fifth delivery only proves that nobody was listening on the first four.
column7: I need to get this out. I've got enough advice already.

column4: Before confiding, people run the maths on afterwards: how this will sit in somebody's memory, how it changes the greeting next time. The calculation is usually correct, which is why so little of it ever gets said.
column7: If I tell them, will they look at me differently after?

column3: The business nobody at home wants to hear about
column4: A founder without a co-founder has nowhere to put the running commentary. Home takes the first year of it and then quietly declines the rest. The decisions keep arriving on schedule, and they start getting made in silence.
column7: There's nobody to talk business with. My family is tired of my topics.

column4: Openness tends to come with a hangover — the sense of having handed something over that can't be collected back. The regret isn't really about what was said. It's about not knowing where it travelled afterwards.
column7: I told a friend and now I wish I hadn't.

column3: The part left out of therapy
column4: Even in good therapy a few things stay outside the room. Being known by somebody every Tuesday makes certain admissions expensive, and the expensive ones are usually the ones that matter. They wait years for somewhere cheaper to be said.
column7: My therapist is good. There are still things I won't say to him.

column4: The need to talk keeps no calendar. It arrives on a Sunday night or halfway through a Tuesday, and the appointment is four days out. By the time the slot comes round the urgency has flattened into something that no longer seems worth the hour.
column7: I need to talk now. I won't make it to Wednesday.

column4: Asking for support is a skill, and plenty of people were raised without it. They can give it out endlessly and take none back, and the gap never reads to anybody as need, because need that stays unvoiced looks exactly like self-sufficiency.
column7: I don't know how to ask anyone for support.

column3: In a town where the car gets recognised
column4: In a small town, walking into a therapist's office is a visible act. The car outside is recognised and the visit becomes information before the first session is over. Privacy stops being a preference there and turns into the deciding factor.
column7: Everyone knows everyone here. I can't be seen going to a therapist.

column4: Running a team comes with a standing requirement to look certain in public, and the requirement doesn't lift at the front door. The uncertainty still exists and has to be held somewhere. Held long enough with nowhere to go, it starts coming out sideways as impatience with the team.
column7: I lead people. I'm not allowed to look shaky.

column3: Someone who knows none of your people
column4: Talking to a friend means talking about people the friend also knows, and every sentence gets edited on the way out for that. A listener with no overlap removes the editing entirely. The first reaction to that is usually suspicion, and relief only comes later.
column7: I want to talk to someone who doesn't know anybody in my life.

column4: Saved Messages has quietly become the place people put what they can't send. It holds everything and returns nothing, so the same thought gets written there in slightly different words for months. Writing something down is a poor substitute for being asked about it.
column7: I write long messages to myself. Nobody ever answers.

column4: After emigrating, the people who understand the context are seven hours out. Their morning is the end of your day, and the conversation that would have helped gets pushed into a window where neither of you is at full strength. Across a year the calls thin out without anybody deciding to stop.
column7: I emigrated. Everyone I'd call is asleep when I need them.
